newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean growers march in support of whiskey tax.
newsitem.headline: Chilean growers march in support of whiskey tax.

text.p: Thousands of people involved in growing grapes used to make a liquor called pisco staged a march Friday to protest foreign pressure on Chile to eliminate a tax on whiskey sales.
The European Union says the tax is a thinly disguised tariff on imported scotch.

Police said about 10,000 people in the northern town of Ovalle, many of them bused in from the surrounding vineyards, marched to demand the government resist what they called European pressure and leave the tax on whiskey in place.
They accused President Eduardo Frei's government of bowing to foreign interests in proposing a gradual reduction of the tax.
"We reject the subordination into which the government has fallen in the face of the whiskey transnationals," said Raul Diaz, president of Chile's main vineyard workers' union.

Chile has long imposed a 70 percent sales tax on all whiskey sales, compared with 25 percent for pisco, a clear and potent brandy-like drink often served with ice or lemon juice. The taxes are levied at point of sale.

The European Union has complained that the tax protects pisco producers unfairly to the detriment of scotch imports. U.S, Canadian and other whiskey makers have also grumbled, but Britain has taken the lead in demanding an end to the tax, which it considers a non-tariff trade barrier.
The European Union council last year began the process of filing an official complaint against Chile in the World Trade Organization (WTO).
The protest in Ovalle, center of Chile's pisco industry, came as the government prepared to send a bill to Congress next week that would scale back the tax.

Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said the government, which is negotiating a free trade agreement with the European Union, was almost sure the bill would be acceptable to the WTO, after an earlier compromise solution last year pleased neither the pisco producers nor the Europeans.
"The important thing is that the bill is compatible with WTO rules, that's our aim. We can't make any guarantees. The European Union might not see things that way," said Insulza.
